2.definition: Historians' term ("gates of power") for the handful of great institutional blocs — the imperial court, the major temples and shrines, and the warrior government — that shared rule in medieval Japan, each checking the others so that none could simply dominate the rest.

The legal system of ancient Rome, which medieval and modern Europe revived and used as the foundation of much of their own law — invoked here as a parallel to how later Japanese military codes built on the Jōei Code.

4.definition: A "virtuous government" act — an official decree cancelling debts and ordering pawned or sold land returned. Used by the shogunate to rescue indebted warriors, it became the standard demand of the peasant uprisings of the next century.

The deliberately belittling title Kublai Khan's envoys used to address Japan's ruler — casting the islands as a mere kingdom owing tribute to the "Emperor of Great Mongolia," rather than a sovereign equal. The same title Yoshimitsu would later accept from Ming China for the sake of trade.

5.definition: The mountain fortress in Kawachi where Kusunoki Masashige's tiny garrison tied down a huge Hōjō army for months in 1333, proving that the Kamakura war machine could be defied and helping bring down the regime.

7.definition: The licensed Sino-Japanese trade Yoshimitsu opened with Ming China, named for the kangō — official split paper tallies a ship had to match against the half held at the Chinese port, distinguishing sanctioned merchants from wakō pirates.

The wooded "northern hills" district on the edge of Kyoto where Yoshimitsu built his gold-leafed retirement villa, the Golden Pavilion. The refined arts of his circle there gave their name to the Kitayama culture of the late 1300s and early 1400s.

8.definition: Medieval Japanese 'leagues' — sworn horizontal alliances of peasants, villagers, or local warriors who banded together to press demands by force, often for tokusei (cancellation of debts).

9.definition: Medieval Japanese 'leagues' — sworn horizontal alliances of peasants, villagers, or local warriors who banded together to press demands by force, often for tokusei (cancellation of debts).

10.definition: The "domain codes" or house laws a Sengoku warlord wrote for his own territory — taxing farmers, settling disputes between retainers, regulating inheritance, and often binding the lord himself, since each domain had become a small independent state with no national law above it.

11.definition: A Buddhist guardian deity worshipped in Japan as an armor-clad god of war and warriors; the warlord Uesugi Kenshin styled himself a living incarnation of him.

The old name for the wild northeastern frontier region of Honshu (the Mutsu/Tōhoku country), far from the capital, where the young warlord Date Masamune carved out one of the largest domains in the country late in the Sengoku.

12.definition: "The realm under heaven" — the whole country united under one ruler. Where most warlords fought to enlarge their own domain, Nobunaga fought, increasingly openly, to take the tenka: all of Japan.

13.definition: Hideyoshi's nationwide survey (taikō kenchi) that measured and registered every rice field by its yield in koku, fixing each farmer to a plot and tax, telling Hideyoshi what every domain owed in soldiers, and helping freeze society into rigid hereditary classes.
